pages.text:
*Rule 17 of the Library at the Bottom of the Sea: One voice makes a candle; a thousand make a sun.*

Ravi cleared his throat, refusing to meet Wren's eyes. His gaze skimmed across the line with the frantic speed of a hawk spotting a field mouse.

"The... lighthouse... keeper... fed... the... goats," he announced, then immediately looked up, waiting for a mark to be placed next to his name.

Wren tapped the rhythm on her knee. Once. Twice. "Wait," she said. "Read it again. Slower."

Ravi blinked. "I read it. It was correct."

"Read it to me," she said. "Not to the clock."

He hesitated, the water around the desk remaining still and dark. Then, with the stiff precision of someone operating a complicated machine, he began again. He stretched each word out, letting them hang in the air.

As he finished, a small string of Glimmers, no longer than a finger, drifted down from the ceiling. It pulsed once with a soft amber glow, then hummed. It was not a sound, but a warmth.

Ravi stared at the light, having never seen a book do that. He looked at Wren, and for the first time, his face was not trying to be something else. It was just listening.
pages.image: Two children sitting side by side on a glowing desk underwater; Wren, in a coral-red sweater, taps her knee while Ravi, in a blue striped shirt, reads from a book as a small string of amber lantern fish glows above them.

pages.text:
"Now you," Wren said.

She held her sea-glass over the next line. The curved piece of glass did not change the words, but it changed the way they moved. Under its shadow, the letters settled. They stopped wriggling and sat down, like students in a quiet class waiting for their turn.

Wren read. It was slow, and it was very slow. She stumbled over the word "mossy" and had to start the sentence again.

Ravi did not look away. He did not check the time. He listened to the sound of the words, the way they bumped into each other, the way "salt" tasted dry and "sea" tasted cold.

Then Wren read the joke about the crab who wore a brass cap.

Ravi snorted. It was a short, sharp laugh, surprising in the quiet water. He looked at the page, then at Wren. "I didn't catch that the first time," he admitted. "I just saw the word 'crab' and moved on."

"Go back," Wren said.

He went back. He read the joke again, just to hear it. He did not do it because it was required. He did it because it was funny, and because it was there.
pages.image: Wren, wearing a coral-red sweater and yellow boots, holds a piece of sea glass over a book while Ravi, in a blue striped shirt, leans in with a surprised smile as they read underwater.

pages.text:
They read together, not racing but talking, trading lines back and forth until the water held every word.

It was like passing a bowl of soup back and forth across a table, no one dropping a spoon, no one rushing. Wren read a sentence, and the water kept it. Ravi read the next, and the water caught that one too.

Above them, the Glimmers did not just glow; they bloomed.

One amber fish lit up. Then ten. Then a hundred. The Lantern Hall, which had been dim and grey for over two hundred years, began to shine. The light spread out in a wide, golden swath, washing over the books, the desks, and the spiral stairs. It was warm and bright, the color of honey, smelling faintly of old paper and salt.

Far away, in the deep, dark corner of the Deep Stacks, the grey silt that was slowly turning the books to sand paused. It curled in on itself, shrinking back from the nearest shelf, retreating from the light.

The Library was breathing again.
pages.image: A vast underwater library hall glowing with golden light from strings of amber fish; two small children sit on a desk in the foreground, reading a book together as the light spreads through the water.

pages.text:
Squib, the small teal cuttlefish, floated near the ceiling. He was bright gold. His wavy pupils were wide with joy. He did a little loop in the water, his tiny brass key swinging.

Then he saw the edge of the light.

The gold stopped at the door. Beyond it, the Deep Stacks were still grey. The silt was still there. The books were still fading.

Squib turned grey. His colors faded, one by one, until he was the color of the silt. He drifted closer to Wren and Ravi, hovering just above their heads.

"It is not enough," he said. His voice was small and watery. "There are three hundred shelves in the Deep Stacks. We have read one chapter."

Ravi looked at the grey silt in the distance. "I can read fast," he said, but his voice lacked its usual stiffness. He sounded worried. "I can read forty more books. I can read all of them. I will count them."

"You are counting," Squib said gently. "But the books do not want to be counted. They want to be heard."

Ravi looked at his hands. He was still holding the book, but he was not looking at the page.
pages.image: A small teal cuttlefish with wavy eyes hovers sadly above two children, its colors fading to grey as it looks toward a dark, shadowy area of the library in the background.

pages.text:
Madame Ottoline drifted into the pool of lantern-light, her eight arms busy. One held a stamp, one an inkwell, and one a silver ribbon bookmark. The other five simply rested, tired but satisfied. She looked at the two children.

"You are both very brave," she said. "And you are both very good."

"But," she continued, her voice rolling in like a deep tide, "a library is not saved by one or two voices. It is saved by a room full of them. By a town. By everyone who has ever felt that a word was too hard or too slow."

Ravi frowned. His fingers twitched on his knee, an old habit from counting pages. He had always counted everything to keep the world in order. But this time, the numbers did not feel like books. They felt like people.

He looked at Wren. Then he looked at the door.

"Saltmarrow," he said slowly. "There are forty children in Room 4. And Mrs. Pell. And my dad. And your dad." He paused. "And the ferry."

He looked up at Ottoline. "How many children are there in Saltmarrow?"
pages.image: A large purple octopus with pince-nez spectacles and a silver ribbon bookmark hovers above two children, looking thoughtful, while Ravi, in a blue striped shirt, looks up with a determined expression.
